1.title: Mitigating Controls and Techniques
1.text: Welcome to Module twelve: Mitigating Controls and Techniques. It covers the exam area Security Operations. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Overview of the toolbox. Deception and disruption technology. Detection and prevention systems and firewalls. Content, endpoint and network access controls. Applications, email and operating systems. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Security Operations (twenty-seven percent). Exam format: up to ninety questions in ninety minutes; a score of seven hundred fifty on a scale of one hundred to nine hundred passes. Validated against: the official Comp T I A Security plus S Y zero eight oh one V eight exam objectives.

1.title: Overview of the toolbox
1.text: Overview of the toolbox. The figure shows this: Mitigations grouped by where they protect: network, endpoint, application, email, identity and data.

1.title: Overview of the toolbox, continued
1.text: Overview of the toolbox. Segmentation. Split the network into zones so an attacker cannot move freely. Access controls. Allow only the right users and devices (module fifteen). Hardening. Remove what is not needed, apply secure settings, patch, change defaults. Sandboxing. Run code in an isolated environment to study or limit it. Monitoring and alerting. Detect problems quickly (module fourteen). Mobile device management (M D M). Enroll, configure and wipe phones and tablets. Application control. Allow lists (only approved apps run) or block lists (known bad apps are blocked). Exam tip: Allow list equals deny everything except what is approved (stronger). Block list equals allow everything except what is listed (weaker). Hardening equals reduce the attack surface.

1.title: Deception and disruption technology
1.text: Deception and disruption technology. Honeypot. A decoy system that attracts attackers. Honeynet. A network of honeypots. Honeyfile. A fake file that raises an alert when opened. Honeytoken. Fake data or credentials that raise an alert when used. Canary account. A fake account that alerts when someone tries to use it. They give early warning and reveal attacker methods.

1.title: Detection and prevention systems and firewalls
1.text: Detection and prevention systems and firewalls. I D S. Detects and alerts. I P S. Detects and blocks. N I D S or N I P S. Network-based sensor on the network. H I D S or H I P S. Host-based, on one computer. W I P S. Wireless intrusion prevention (rogue access points). Firewall. Filters traffic by rules; layer four (ports, protocols) or layer seven (application content). Rate limiting. Caps requests per time to slow floods and brute force. waff. Web application firewall protects web apps from injection and cross-site scripting. Rule-based. Traffic matched against ordered rules; ends with an implicit deny. U T M. Unified threat management: firewall plus I P S, filtering and antivirus in one device. Exam tip: I P S blocks, I D S only alerts. A waff protects web applications at layer seven. A U T M combines several functions in one appliance.

1.title: Content, endpoint and network access controls
1.text: Content, endpoint and network access controls. Content filter. Blocks bad sites and content. Data loss prevention (D L P). Stops sensitive data leaving; agent-based (on the endpoint) or via a centralized proxy. E D R. Endpoint detection and response: records endpoint behavior, detects, isolates and remediates. X D R. Extended detection and response: combines endpoint, network, email and cloud signals. Antivirus. Detects known malware by signatures and behavior. Network access control (N A C). Decides who may connect; captive portals (a sign-in page), eight oh two dot one X (port-based authentication), endpoint posture checks.

1.title: Applications, email and operating systems
1.text: Applications, email and operating systems. Repositories. Secrets scanning finds keys and passwords in code. Application security. Input validation, secure cookies, static code analysis, code signing. Email security. S P F (which servers may send for a domain), dee kim (signs messages), dee mark (policy and reporting using S P F and dee kim), bim ee (shows a verified brand logo). Operating system security. Group Policy (central Windows settings), S E Linux (mandatory access control on Linux).

1.title: Applications, email and operating systems, continued
1.text: Applications, email and operating systems. The figure shows this: S P F, dee kim and dee mark: who may send, signed messages, and what to do when checks fail. Exam tip: S P F lists allowed sending servers; dee kim gives a signature; dee mark tells receivers what to do when S P F or dee kim fail and sends reports. Code signing proves who wrote code and that it is unchanged.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors wants only approved programs to run on kiosk computers. Which control fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: An application allow list. An allow list permits only approved applications, which is stronger than blocking known bad ones.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A fake database account has no real use, and any sign-in attempt on it triggers an alert. What is it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Canary account. A canary account is a decoy that alerts when anyone tries to use it.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Which device both detects malicious traffic and blocks it automatically on the network? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: N I P S. A network-based intrusion prevention system detects and blocks, while an I D S only alerts.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A web shop wants to filter sequel injection attempts at the application layer. Which control fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: waff. A web application firewall inspects layer seven web traffic for injection and similar attacks.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A domain owner wants receivers to reject mail that fails S P F and dee kim checks and to receive reports. Which record does this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: dee mark. dee mark sets the policy for failed checks and provides reporting.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A tool records process activity on laptops, detects suspicious behavior and can isolate a laptop. Which solution is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: E D R. Endpoint detection and response monitors endpoints and can contain compromised ones.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is hardening? Answer: Reducing the attack surface by removing unneeded features and applying secure settings. Question two. What is the difference between a honeypot and a honeytoken? Answer: A honeypot is a decoy system; a honeytoken is fake data or credentials that alert when used. Question three. What do S P F, dee kim and dee mark do? Answer: S P F lists allowed senders, dee kim signs messages, dee mark sets policy and reporting.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What does eight oh two dot one X provide? Answer: Port-based network access authentication. Question five. What does X D R add to E D R? Answer: Correlation across endpoint, network, email and cloud signals. Question six. What does secrets scanning find? Answer: Keys, tokens and passwords stored in code repositories.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Basics: segmentation, access control, hardening, sandboxing, M D M, allow lists (strong) and block lists. Deception: honeypot, honeynet, honeyfile, honeytoken, canary account. Detection and filtering: I D S alerts, I P S blocks; N I D S or N I P S, H I D S or H I P S, W I P S. Endpoint and access: D L P, E D R, X D R, antivirus; N A C (captive portal, eight oh two dot one X, posture). Apps, email, O S: secrets scanning, input validation, secure cookies, static analysis, code signing; S P F, dee kim, dee mark, bim ee. In the next module, we continue the course.
